nodes.label: Sassanid Persia
nodes.full: The empire the Nasrids serve for three centuries: it grants their autonomy, pays their subsidy, uses their cavalry against Rome, fosters its own princes at al-Hira, and finally — under Khosrow II — executes the last king and puts a governor in his place.
nodes.src: background — see the sassanid-224-484 / sassanid-484-651 folios; Rothstein, 'Die Dynastie der Lahmiden' (1899)

nodes.label: The Ghassanids
nodes.full: The mirror Arab client kingdom on the Byzantine side. The Lakhmid–Ghassanid proxy war runs across the Syrian steppe for a century; al-Mundhir III sacrifices al-Harith's son at the shrine of al-Uzza, and al-Harith kills al-Mundhir III at Yawm Halima in revenge.
nodes.src: background — see the ghassanid-420-638 folio; Shahid, 'Byzantium and the Arabs' (BASIC)

nodes.label: Byzantium
nodes.full: Rome's eastern empire — the enemy the Lakhmid cavalry raids on Persia's behalf, and the territory in which Imru al-Qays's tombstone was raised, hinting he changed sides.
nodes.src: background — Procopius, 'Wars'; Socrates Scholasticus, 'HE'

nodes.label: The Islamic state
nodes.full: The Arab-Muslim polity out of the Hijaz that pours through the frontier the abolition of the Lakhmid kingdom had opened, wins the first Arab victory over Persia at Dhu Qar, and takes al-Hira by negotiated surrender in the 630s.
nodes.src: background — Kennedy, 'The Great Arab Conquests' (2007); al-Baladhuri, 'Futuh al-Buldan'

nodes.label: Amr ibn Adi
nodes.full: Traditional founder of the Lakhmid kingdom at al-Hira; mentioned in a Pahlavi/Parthian inscription and a Coptic text — the two earliest hard anchors for the dynasty.
nodes.src: Identified as 'Amr ibn Lakhm' in two pre-Islamic inscriptions: one Pahlavi/Parthian, one Coptic — cited by Schiettecatte & Arbach (2016). Later Arabic tradition: Hisham al-Kalbi (d.819), drawing on al-Hira records. Dates approximate.

nodes.label: Imru al-Qays ibn Amr
nodes.full: Calls himself 'King of all the Arabs' on his tombstone — the Namara inscription of 328 CE, found in Roman-controlled southern Syria, not Sasanian territory; this location strongly suggests he defected to Rome during his career, making him both the most epigraphically documented early Lakhmid and a figure of ambiguous political allegiance.
nodes.src: HARD ANCHOR: Namara inscription, basalt stele, dated 7 Dec 328 CE (internal calendar date). Found Namara, Syria 1901 — in Roman territory, not Sasanian. Now Louvre (inv. AO 4083). Nabataean-Arabic script; contains first known use of 'king of all the Arabs' (malik jami al-Arab). Robin (2010) on the Roman territory implication. Irfan Shahid: 'the most important Arabic inscription of pre-Islamic times.'

nodes.label: Amr II ibn Imru al-Qays
nodes.full: Reigned through the period of Julian's Persian war; al-Hira close enough to the Roman-Persian frontier that Lakhmid forces likely participated in Sasanian defence.
nodes.src: Source: Hisham al-Kalbi king list (9th c., drawing on al-Hira records). Dates uncertain by ±10 years. No contemporary non-Arabic source corroborates this reign specifically. Rothstein (1899) Die Dynastie der Lahmiden is the foundational study.

nodes.label: Aws ibn Qallam
nodes.full: A non-Nasrid interlude — a Christian Arab nobleman who briefly displaced the dynasty, then was killed in a Lakhmid nobleman's revolt restoring Nasrid rule.
nodes.src: Source: Hisham al-Kalbi. Rothstein (1899) p.64. Aws described as scion of a Christian Arab family; a relative built a church at al-Hira. Dates uncertain.

nodes.label: Imru al-Qays II ibn Amr
nodes.full: Nestorian Christian; restored Nasrid rule after the Aws interlude. Little documented beyond his religion and approximate dates.
nodes.src: Source: Hisham al-Kalbi. Religion: Nestorian Christianity noted in Arabic sources. Chronology approximate per Rothstein (1899). No contemporary external corroboration for this specific reign.

nodes.label: al-Numan I ibn Imru al-Qays
nodes.full: Builder of the legendary palaces Khawarnaq (built for the Sasanian prince Bahram Gur) and Sadir — both praised in pre-Islamic Arabic poetry as wonders of the world.
nodes.src: Palaces: Khawarnaq and Sadir named in multiple Arabic poetic sources (Adi ibn Zayd, al-Nabigha). Encyclopaedia Iranica (Bosworth). Dates from Hisham al-Kalbi. The palace of Khawarnaq is the subject of a famous qasida by al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī.

nodes.label: al-Mundhir I ibn al-Numan
nodes.full: Fought for the Persians against the Byzantines and played a role in the Sasanian succession crisis of 420 — corroborated by the Greek church historian Socrates Scholasticus.
nodes.src: CORROBORATED: Socrates Scholasticus HE 7.18 (c.440) mentions al-Mundhir as commander of Lakhmid troops in 421–422 without calling him king. Shahid, BASIC I.1 (1989). Duration from Hisham al-Kalbi.

nodes.label: al-Aswad ibn al-Mundhir
nodes.full: Brief reign following his father al-Mundhir I; the 5th century is better documented than the 4th but dates remain approximate within a decade.
nodes.src: Source: Hisham al-Kalbi. Partial corroboration from Syriac chronicles of the period. Shahid, BASIC I.1 (1989) pp.31–40.

nodes.label: al-Numan II ibn al-Aswad
nodes.full: Long reign bridging the middle and late periods; his son al-Mundhir III will become the most powerful Lakhmid king.
nodes.src: Source: Hisham al-Kalbi. Dates partially corroborated by Syriac chronicle material. Rothstein (1899); Shahid, BASIC I.2 (1989).

nodes.label: al-Mundhir III ibn al-Numan
nodes.full: The most powerful Lakhmid king — reigned 50 years, fought the Ghassanids repeatedly, extended Sasanian influence across Arabia, and died at the Battle of Yawm Halima in 554.
nodes.src: WELL DOCUMENTED: Procopius Wars 1.17, 2.1, 2.16 (Greek, contemporary). Syriac Chronicle of Pseudo-Zacharias Rhetor. Died at Yawm Halima 554 — multiple Arabic sources; Shahid, BASIC I.2 pp.195–260. Dates confirmed by cross-reference with Byzantine sources.

nodes.label: Amr ibn Hind
nodes.full: Notoriously arrogant king celebrated and condemned in Arabic poetry; patron of the poet Tarafa, whom he executed — the most vivid portrait of a Lakhmid king in the literary record.
nodes.src: LITERARY ANCHOR: Tarafa ibn al-Abd's Muallaqat (one of the Seven Odes) — composed at Amr ibn Hind's court, terminus ante quem 569. Al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani's odes addressed to Amr ibn Hind survive. Tabari I.948–950. Montgomery (2012), Arabian Poet.

nodes.label: al-Mundhir IV ibn al-Mundhir
nodes.full: Son of al-Mundhir III; his short reign is a transition between the dynasty's peak and its final collapse under Khosrow II.
nodes.src: Source: Tabari I; Hisham al-Kalbi. Dates partly corroborated by Byzantine sources mentioning Lakhmid activity. Shahid, BASIC II.1 (1995).

nodes.label: al-Numan III ibn al-Mundhir
nodes.full: Last Lakhmid king — converted to Nestorian Christianity, was betrayed to Khosrow II (possibly over the Adi ibn Zayd affair), then executed by being trampled to death by elephants c.602, ending the dynasty after over 300 years of Sasanian service.
nodes.src: WELL DOCUMENTED: Tabari I.1012–1022 (most detailed; records execution by elephant trampling). Al-Numan's Christianity: multiple Arabic sources. Death c.602 at Ctesiphon: Tabari. Adi ibn Zayd connection: Ibn al-Kalbi. Bosworth (1999) EI2 s.v. al-Numan ibn al-Mundhir. End of kingdom: Tabari I.1022; Dinawari, Akhbar al-Tiwal. The elephant execution: also in Ibn Abd Rabbih, al-Iqd al-Farid.

nodes.label: Yawm Halima — death of al-Mundhir III
nodes.full: Al-Mundhir III killed by the Ghassanid king al-Harith ibn Jabalah in revenge for the sacrifice of al-Harith's son ten years earlier — named 'the Day of Halima' after al-Harith's daughter who rallied her side's warriors.
nodes.src: Arabic sources: Tabari I.948; Aghani preserves poetic accounts. The revenge motive: explicit in Arabic tradition — al-Harith acts to avenge his sacrificed son (c.544 event). Named after Halima, daughter of al-Harith. Irfan Shahid, BASIC I.2 pp.195–260. Date c.554 confirmed by Byzantine synchronism with Procopius.

nodes.label: al-Mundhir III raids Byzantine Syria
nodes.full: Al-Mundhir III leads a devastating raid into Byzantine Syria reaching the outskirts of Antioch — Procopius describes it as leaving a trail of destruction the Romans could not halt.
nodes.src: Procopius Wars 2.1.4–5 (contemporary Greek source). Shahid, BASIC I.2 pp.128–140. Date 529 from Procopius's narrative context; consistent with Malalas Chronicle.

nodes.label: Ain Ubagh — al-Mundhir III sacrifices son of al-Harith
nodes.full: Al-Mundhir III captures a son of the Ghassanid king al-Harith ibn Jabalah and sacrifices him at the shrine of al-Uzza — a deliberate act of ritual humiliation; al-Harith survives and takes revenge ten years later at Yawm Halima (c.554) where Mundhir is killed.
nodes.src: Procopius Wars 2.28.13 (contemporary, most detailed Greek account) records the sacrifice at a pagan sanctuary. Tabari I.948. The victim was al-Harith's son, not al-Harith himself — a distinction blurred in some sources. The two events (544 sacrifice; 554 revenge killing) are separated by a decade in the sources. Shahid, BASIC I.2 pp.176–195.

nodes.label: Lakhmid forces in the Roman-Persian wars
nodes.full: Lakhmid troops serve as Sasanian auxiliaries in successive Roman-Persian wars — the primary military purpose of the client kingdom from a Persian perspective.
nodes.src: 421–422: Socrates Scholasticus HE 7.18 (al-Mundhir I as commander). 502–506: Procopius Wars 1.8–9. 527–531: Procopius Wars 1.17–18. The Lakhmid military role in these campaigns is the best-documented aspect of the kingdom's external relations.

nodes.label: Abolition of the Lakhmid kingdom
nodes.full: Khosrow II has al-Numan III executed and replaces the Lakhmid king with a Persian-appointed governor — removing the desert buffer that had protected Persia for three centuries.
nodes.src: Tabari I.1022 (the standard account). Dinawari, Akhbar al-Tiwal. The decision's strategic consequences: the removed buffer allowed Arab tribes free movement, contributing to the ease of the 630s Islamic conquest. Bosworth (1999) EI2.

nodes.label: Battle of Dhu Qar
nodes.full: Arab tribal forces defeat a Sassanid army near al-Hira — the first Arab victory over Persia, fought in the power vacuum left by the abolition of the Lakhmid kingdom.
nodes.src: Tabari I.1030–1040 (most detailed account). Date disputed: 604, 606 or 610 in different sources. The battle's symbolic importance was enormous — celebrated as proof Arab forces could defeat Persia. Authenticity accepted by most scholars; Caskel (1954).

nodes.label: Al-Hira as Sasanian administrative hub
nodes.full: Al-Hira serves as the Sasanian Empire's interface with the Arab tribal world — Adi ibn Zayd and his brothers held the official position of 'secretaries of Arab affairs' at the Sasanian court.
nodes.src: Adi ibn Zayd's role: Tabari I.1000–1005; Toral-Niehoff (2008) p.239. The secretarial function is the clearest evidence of how the Lakhmid-Sasanian administrative relationship worked in practice.

nodes.label: Sasanian grant of autonomy to Lakhmids
nodes.full: The Lakhmids retained their own laws, language and religious practices under Sasanian suzerainty — a formally documented client relationship distinguishing them from direct Sasanian provinces.
nodes.src: The client relationship's legal structure is inferred from Procopius Wars 1.17 (Greek), Tabari's account of the relationship, and the contrast with directly administered Sasanian territories. Rothstein (1899); Encyclopaedia Iranica (Bosworth).

nodes.label: Church of the East synod at al-Hira
nodes.full: A synod of the Church of the East (Nestorian) is held at al-Hira — one of several Church councils documented at the Lakhmid capital, confirming its importance as a Christian centre.
nodes.src: Synodicon Orientale (Chabot edition, 1902): synod records survive in Syriac. Date 554 internally confirmed. Fiey (1965) on the Church of the East in Mesopotamia. Al-Hira's bishopric is documented from the 5th century onward.

nodes.label: Al-Hira as a major Nestorian centre
nodes.full: Al-Hira is home to a Nestorian bishop from at least the early 5th century — the Church of the East uses it as a base for missionary activity in the Persian Gulf and Eastern Arabia.
nodes.src: Synodicon Orientale (Syriac; Chabot 1902): al-Hira's bishop listed from 410 synod. Fiey (1965) Assyrie chrétienne. The bishopric's role in Gulf missions: Potts (1990), The Arabian Gulf in Antiquity.

nodes.label: Al-Numan III converts to Christianity
nodes.full: The last Lakhmid king publicly converts to Nestorian Christianity — possibly after the peace with Byzantium in 591; his conversion enhanced al-Hira's status as a Christian missionary hub.
nodes.src: Conversion after 591 peace: Shahid, BASIC II.1 (1995) pp.119–120. Multiple Arabic sources note al-Numan as Christian. The connection to the 591 Byzantine-Persian peace is argued by Shahid but disputed by others.

nodes.label: Pagan cult and the oscillation of kings
nodes.full: Several Lakhmid kings oscillate between paganism and Christianity — some are pagan, some Christian, some ambiguous; al-Mundhir III performs a human sacrifice at a pagan sanctuary in 554.
nodes.src: Human sacrifice: Procopius Wars 2.28.13 (contemporary). Oscillation documented across Tabari and Arabic sources. Trimingham (1979), Christianity Among the Arabs. The religious ambiguity at al-Hira is a major scholarly discussion: Toral-Niehoff (2010).

nodes.label: Synod of Isaac 410 — al-Hira established as major diocese
nodes.full: The first great synod of the Church of the East in 410 lists a bishop of al-Hira among its signatories — establishing the Lakhmid capital as a major diocese and the primary institutional base for Nestorian Christianity in Arabia; the earliest hard documentary evidence for Christian institutional presence at al-Hira.
nodes.src: Synodicon Orientale, Synod of Isaac 410 (Syriac text; Chabot 1902 critical edition). The bishop of al-Hira is listed among signatories. This is the earliest certain documentary evidence for Christianity at al-Hira.

nodes.label: Palace of Khawarnaq
nodes.full: Built by al-Numan I for the Sasanian prince Bahram Gur during his upbringing at al-Hira — praised in pre-Islamic Arabic poetry as a wonder of the world, not yet archaeologically identified.
nodes.src: Literary source: al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani's ode on Khawarnaq (surviving poem, 6th c. but describing 5th c. tradition). Also: Adi ibn Zayd's poem. Massignon identified a probable site. Encyclopaedia Iranica (Bosworth) s.v. Khawarnaq.

nodes.label: Tarafa ibn al-Abd: Muallaqat ode
nodes.full: One of the Seven Hanging Odes (Muallaqat) — the pre-Islamic Arabic poetic canon; composed at the Lakhmid court, it is the finest surviving example of 6th-century Arabic qasida poetry.
nodes.src: Text survives in multiple medieval manuscripts; printed editions from 19th c. onward. Montgomery (2012), The Muallaqat. Tarafa executed by Amr ibn Hind — the ode itself contains veiled critique of the king. Terminus ante quem: 569 (Amr's death).

nodes.label: Al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani (c.535–604): court odes to Lakhmids
nodes.full: Al-Nabigha (c.535–604) serves at both the Lakhmid and Ghassanid courts alternately — his surviving odes addressed to Amr ibn Hind and al-Numan III are primary sources for 6th-century court culture, and his lifespan spanning the dynasty's final decades makes him its last major literary witness.
nodes.src: Poems survive in the Aghani (al-Isfahani, 10th c.) and Diwans (collected works). Arberry (1957), The Seven Odes. The odes' historical references (battles, court events) have been cross-referenced with other sources by Shahid, BASIC II.1.

nodes.label: Adi ibn Zayd: prison poems
nodes.full: Christian Arab poet and Sasanian court secretary imprisoned by al-Numan III; his prison poems are among the most personal pre-Islamic Arabic texts, combining wine poetry with theological reflection.
nodes.src: Poems survive in Aghani and the Diwan of Adi ibn Zayd. Toral-Niehoff (2008) critical study. Imprisonment and execution c.600: Tabari I.1005–1010. Adi's poems are the richest internal literary source for late Lakhmid court culture.

nodes.label: Sasanian silver plate at al-Hira
nodes.full: Al-Hira was a major distribution point for Sasanian luxury silver — plates and vessels found across the Arabian peninsula reflect the material culture of the Lakhmid court and its gift economy.
nodes.src: Gunter & Jett (1992), Ancient Iranian Metalwork in the Arthur M. Sackler Gallery. The distribution of Sasanian silver in Arabia is partly mapped through find-spots. Al-Hira itself has limited archaeological excavation (Harper 1978).

nodes.label: Al-Hira as the birthplace of Arab classical music
nodes.full: Al-Hira's court musicians absorb Persian lute tuning and technique via Sassanid influence — the barbat becomes the Arab 'ud, the modal system is adopted, and the qiyan (singing girls) of al-Hira transmit the repertoire to the Hijaz; this makes al-Hira the direct origin point of classical Arab music.
nodes.src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Islamic Arts (Music History): 'The culture of al-Hirah under the Lakhmid dynasty was closely connected with that of Persia under the Sassanid empire. Persian lute tuning was adopted for the lute (ʿūd), which became the classical instrument of the Arabs.' Farmer (1929), A History of Arabian Music: the foundational study, documents the al-Hira transmission. The qiyan of al-Hira: Cambridge Core (2012), Gender and the Politics of Music in the Early Islamic Courts. The 'ud's Persian origin via al-Hira: al-Islam.org, History of Muslim Philosophy Vol.2 ch.57.

nodes.label: Hisham al-Kalbi: king list of al-Hira
nodes.full: Ibn al-Kalbi's king list is the backbone of Lakhmid chronology — compiled in the early 9th century but explicitly drawing on records kept at al-Hira itself; the 2022 Shahid study confirms it is reliable where it can be checked.
nodes.src: Hisham al-Kalbi (d.819/821): Jamharat al-Nasab. King list assessed by Shahid (2022, ResearchGate): 'periods of rule as in Hisham al-Kalbi's list are to be accepted as reliable evidence for they appear to go back to primary sources from al-Hira.' Rothstein (1899) first critical use.

nodes.label: Tabari: Annals on the Lakhmid kings
nodes.full: Al-Tabari's vast Annals contain the most detailed narrative of Lakhmid history in Arabic — drawn from earlier sources including Ibn al-Kalbi; invaluable for the 6th-century kings but epistemically a secondary source.
nodes.src: Al-Tabari (d.923), Tarikh al-Rusul wa'l-Muluk. English translation: Bosworth (1999), vol. V, The Sasanids, the Byzantines, the Lakhmids and Yemen. Primary compilation ~915 CE. Earlier sources identified and assessed by Nöldeke (1879).

nodes.label: Arabic script develops at al-Hira and al-Anbar
nodes.full: The Arabic alphabet as we know it is attributed by medieval Arab scholars to scribes working at al-Hira and the nearby town of al-Anbar — the literate bilingual (Arabic-Persian) scribal class of the Lakhmid court is the most plausible vector for the Nabataean-to-Arabic script transition already visible in the Namara inscription.
nodes.src: Ibn al-Nadim, Fihrist (987 CE) 1.4: explicitly attributes the development of the Arabic script to the people of al-Hira and al-Anbar. The Nabataean-Arabic transition visible in the Namara inscription (328 CE, Louvre AO 4083) is the earliest physical evidence. Al-Marzubani and others corroborate the al-Hira attribution. Abbott (1939), The Rise of the North Arabic Script (University of Chicago): the foundational modern study. The claim is broadly accepted in scholarship though details are debated.

nodes.label: Sasanian tributary relationship
nodes.full: The Lakhmids received Sasanian subsidy in exchange for frontier defence — the reverse of a tax relationship; Procopius records that the Persians paid the Ghassanids and Lakhmids for their services.
nodes.src: Procopius Wars 1.17.47 records Sasanian payments to Lakhmid and other Arab client rulers. Shahid, BASIC I.1 pp.115–120. The precise terms are not documented in a surviving treaty text.

nodes.label: Al-Hira as Arabian trade entrepôt
nodes.full: Al-Hira sits at the junction of the Euphrates trade system and the overland Arabian routes — a key node connecting the Sassanid economy with the Arabian peninsula's tribal networks and the Indian Ocean trade beyond.
nodes.src: Trade role: inferred from al-Hira's geography and the caravan poetry of the period. Potts (1990), The Arabian Gulf in Antiquity. Direct documentary evidence is sparse — the trade function is argued from material culture and literary references rather than papyri or inscriptions. MOVED from Economy s1.

nodes.label: Bahram Gur raised at al-Hira — Persian-Arab cultural bond
nodes.full: The future Sassanid emperor Bahram V grows up at the Lakhmid court — returning to Ctesiphon with Lakhmid military backing to claim his throne; the most concrete instance of the Lakhmid-Sassanid relationship producing direct political consequences.
nodes.src: Tabari I.848–855. Bahram's upbringing at al-Hira corroborated by Socrates Scholasticus HE 7.18. Bahram gained the Sassanid throne 420 with Lakhmid support against Persian nobles — documented in Tabari and confirmed in spirit by Socrates. MOVED from World w2.

nodes.label: Al-Hira as transmission centre for pre-Islamic Arabic poetry
nodes.full: Al-Hira's scribal tradition — bilingual in Arabic and Persian — preserves and transmits the pre-Islamic poetic corpus to Islamic-era collectors; the Muallaqat and other canonical odes survive because they passed through al-Hira's literate culture.
nodes.src: Toral-Niehoff (2010), al-Hira as paradigmatic third space. The scribal tradition: Adi ibn Zayd's family served as court secretaries in both Arabic and Persian. Al-Hira's role in Arabic literary transmission: Beeston (1983), Arabic Literature to the End of the Umayyad Period. MOVED from Thought t3.

nodes.label: Lakhmid-Ghassanid rivalry as proxy war
nodes.full: The Lakhmids (Sasanian clients) and Ghassanids (Byzantine clients) fight a decades-long proxy war across the Syrian steppe — the most sustained documented Arab geopolitical rivalry before Islam.
nodes.src: Procopius Wars (multiple books, contemporary). Shahid, BASIC I.2 and II.1 are the comprehensive modern studies. The rivalry structured Arab politics from c.500 until the abolition of both client kingdoms (Lakhmids 602, Ghassanids effectively 584).

nodes.label: Abolition creates the vacuum for Islamic conquest
nodes.full: The removal of the Lakhmid buffer in 602 left the Sasanian western flank exposed to Arab tribal raiding — within a generation this vacuum becomes the corridor for the Islamic conquest of Iraq (633–637).
nodes.src: The strategic consequence: Tabari I.1022 (explicit). Kennedy (2007), The Great Arab Conquests, ch.4. The causal connection between Lakhmid abolition and Islamic conquest is a historiographic consensus, not just Arabic tradition.

nodes.label: Namara inscription — earliest Arabic literary text
nodes.full: The tombstone of Imru al-Qays ibn Amr, dated to the day, is one of the earliest Arabic language texts — it places the Lakhmids at the intersection of Nabataean, Arabic and proto-Islamic epigraphy.
nodes.src: Louvre AO 4083. Basalt, 7 Dec 328. Nabataean-Arabic script. First published: Dussaud & Macler (1901). Critical studies: Bellamy (1985), Robin (2010). Irfan Shahid: 'the most important Arabic inscription of pre-Islamic times.' Now a key text in Arabic linguistic history.

nodes.label: Al-Hira falls to the Islamic state
nodes.full: Khalid ibn al-Walid captures al-Hira in 633 (or 638 — sources differ); the Lakhmid capital negotiates surrender rather than resist, its Christian population pays the jizya tax, and the city transitions into the early Islamic administrative network — within a generation it is eclipsed by the new garrison city of Kufa founded nearby.
nodes.src: Tabari I (Arabic, most detailed on the conquest). Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan: records al-Hira's negotiated surrender and jizya terms. Date disputed: 633 in most Arabic sources, but 638 in some modern reconstructions. Kennedy (2007), The Great Arab Conquests, ch.5. The foundation of Kufa (637/638) as the replacement centre: confirmed in multiple sources. Al-Hira's rapid eclipse documented in geographical literature by the 9th century.

nodes.label: Hind bint al-Nu'man — documented queen of al-Hira
nodes.full: Hind, daughter of al-Nu'man III, is documented in Arabic sources as a significant cultural figure at al-Hira — her Christian convents, her patronage of poets, and her exchanges with the early Muslim community give her more textual presence than almost any pre-Islamic Arab woman.
nodes.src: Hind's convents at al-Hira: multiple Arabic sources. Her meeting with the Prophet Muhammad: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat. Aghani (al-Isfahani) preserves stories of her patronage. Shahid, BASIC II.1 (1995) pp.427–430. The evidence is later Arabic tradition, not contemporary, but internally consistent. She is the best-evidenced named woman in the Lakhmid corpus.

nodes.label: Mukhannathun in pre-Islamic court culture
nodes.full: The courts of al-Hira and the Ghassanids both employed mukhannathun as musicians and entertainers — the earliest context for this recognised gender-variant role that will later be explicitly documented in early Islamic Medina.
nodes.src: The al-Hira connection: Toral-Niehoff (2010), al-Hira as cultural transmission centre. Rowson (1991) traces the mukhannathun category back through the al-Hira court tradition. The evidence is indirect — the court music tradition at al-Hira is documented (Adi ibn Zayd, Barbad's later training), and the mukhannathun role within it is inferred from the early Islamic sources that describe the tradition they inherited.

nodes.label: Al-Khansa — the greatest pre-Islamic Arab poet
nodes.full: Al-Khansa bint Amr composes the most celebrated elegies in pre-Islamic Arabic poetry — for her brothers killed in battle; she later converts to Islam and is praised by the Prophet; her documented public poetic career is the strongest evidence for female intellectual agency in the pre-Islamic Arab world.
nodes.src: Al-Khansa's Diwan (collected poems): multiple medieval manuscript traditions; printed edition (Beirut 1888). Her meeting with the Prophet: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat al-Kubra 8.273–277. Her performance at the Ukaz market: documented in the Aghani. Arberry (1957) translation. The Diwan is the most substantial body of work by a pre-Islamic woman in any language from this region.
